newsitem.title: UK: UK Conservatives under fire over nurseries.
newsitem.headline: UK Conservatives under fire over nurseries.

text.p: Britain's ruling Conservatives, already under fire over their handling of food safety and trailing in polls with the election rapidly approaching, have been criticised for one of their key education policies.
A leaked all-party report said there was no clear evidence the government's nursery voucher scheme boosted parental choice.

Instead, the House of Commons Education Committee report said, the scheme badly affected playgroups run by volunteers, some of which were forced to close as local primary schools increased the number of places for four year olds.
As a result, parental choice was cut and not increased.

Estelle Morris, the opposition Labour party's spokeswoman on early education, said the voucher idea -- trumpeted by the Conservatives as one of their flagship policies distinguishing them from the opposition -- was "an expensive failure".
Attacking the government for planning to extend the four regional pilot projects nationwide despite the criticism, she said the schemes were "a cruel con...They are a waste of money."
But the government's schools minister Robin Squire dismissed the committee's reported conclusions, saying "the facts are wrong...There has been an expansion in the number of places."

Conservative and minority Liberal Democrat members of the parliamentary committee also criticised the leaking of the report, pointing the finger at Labour who they said were seeking to wring a pre-election advantage out of the report.
The report was only agreed late on Wednesday afternoon, after hours of wrangling in the committee, where some Conservative members tried to soften the criticism.
But the majority of ruling party's members agreed that the report should reflect the findings of the committee's inquiry.
The scheme is designed to give parents the choice of education for their four-year-olds, offering them vouchers which can be redeemed in voluntary, private or state nurseries.
Most of the money is from existing resources which would otherwise have been given to local education authorities to expand state school nursery schemes.

Labour, which aims to offer all four-year-olds nursery education through partnership between the local authorities and voluntary groups if -- as polls forecast -- it wins the election, say the scheme is bureaucratic and wasteful.
The row is just the latest argument over policy to hobbled Prime Minister John Major's efforts to cut Labour's poll lead.
With an election due by May at the latest, Major faces a herculean task hauling in Labour's 20 point poll lead. -- London Newsroom +44 171 542 7768
